newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland checking if Swiss banks transferred cash.
newsitem.headline: Poland checking if Swiss banks transferred cash.

text.p: Poland aims to reveal details shortly of 1949 arrangements under which dormant Swiss bank accounts of Polish citizens were to be transferred to Warsaw's central bank, a foreign ministry spokesman said on Monday.

"We are not sure yet whether money was actually transferred to Poland," spokesman Pawel Dobrowolski said, adding that his ministry was studying the relevant documents and had asked the National Bank of Poland to check its records.

The office of U.S. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato has alleged the deal, involving assets of Jews murdered in the Holocaust, opened the way for Swiss citizens to get compensation from Warsaw for property seized in then-communist Poland.

On Friday Switzerland acknowledged that it struck a confidential deal with Poland in 1949 to liquidate Polish citizens' unclaimed wealth, but denied the money had been used to compensate Swiss citizens.
Jewish activists say most of the money belonged to Jews who had placed it in Switzerland for safe-keeping before World War Two German invaders killed most of Poland's 3.5 million Jews.
World Jewish Congress (WJC) officials have demanded that Switzerland pay millions of dollars in compensation to the World Jewish Restitution Organisation.
A 1949 bilateral treaty publicly called for Poland to pay Switzerland 52.1 million Swiss francs ($41 million at 1996 rates) for property the then-communist regime had seized.

An unpublished exchange of letters, now acknowledged by Switzerland, at the same time agreed that Polish citizens' Swiss bank accounts and life insurance policies that went unclaimed for five years would be turned over to Poland.
The Swiss foreign minister in 1950 cited estimates of the sums involved in this exchange at around two million Swiss francs, according to document found by a U.S. Jewish group.
The Polish foreign ministry's Dobrowolski told Reuters he understood unofficially that this was about the real amount.
"It is in the range of two million francs," he said.
He said the ministry was trying to discover whether any claims had later been placed by owners or their heirs to some of this money, or whether such claims could now still be valid.
"The status of any claims on this money, past or future, is still unclear," Dobrowolski said.

Meanwhile, the Polish official who negotiated compensation to Switzerland said the understanding on dormant accounts had been reached by another Polish team and the issues had not been directly linked during those talks which he himself conducted.

"I was informed of this, but what was in those letters I don't know and I have no idea whether there were any actions to carry out those decisions," former senior Polish treasury ministry official Leon Kurowski told Reuters.
He said that under the compensation agreement, Poland was to pay Switzerland promptly with coal, of which it had plenty while the rest of Europe faced shortages.
"It was clearly stated that compensation, to the sum mentioned of 50 plus million Swiss francs, would be paid out in the form of coal supplies," Kurowski said in Warsaw.
"I assume this happened, but not long after this agreement I ended my cooperation with the government and I was not informed about any implementation," he added.
